content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores continual learning models from the perspective of trying to maximize fine tuning accuracy for the models as training goes on. They show that as more tasks are trained on, the fine tuned accuracy on future tasks increases. They also propose a method called Global Attention Discretization (GLAD) that performs training on current tasks to increase generalization on future tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper's focus on learning generalizable features for future tasks is an interesting lens to view the problem of continual learning.
Weaknesses:
- This paper claims to introduce a new setting called Continual Pre-training which they say is different from past literature. I am not convinced this is the case. The setting is the same as previous works, the only difference is that this paper decides to solely focus on trying to create generalizable representations and not on the problem of maintaining performance on previous tasks. Optimizing for a different metric doesn't really change the setting.
- The metrics used to evaluate and analyze the different methods in this paper (final acc, fwd transfer) are not precisely defined. What is the protocol to compute them? Attention distance is also used in multiple plots, but I don't see it defined.
- This paper is a bit hard to read. Both lower level language choices and higher level organization of the paper could be improved. For example, the specific method that is being proposed (GLAD) could be better motivated and explained. Currently, there is just a section that has the objective function for the method, but the motivation for how it was arrived at is hard to find. The specific details of the objective function are also missing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper needs to make significant revisions to improve its clarity. Several metrics are used in the paper without being properly defined. The overall objective for their proposed method needs to be better motivated. The paper also has some issues with originality, as I'd argue that their contribution of a new setting is more just a focus on different metrics.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is difficult to read and is missing a lot of details of their metrics and method. In its current state, I would not recommend acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on continual self-supervised learning using vision transformers based on the masked image modeling (MIM) setting.  It presents a module termed GLAD (Global Attention Discretization) which regularizes the multi-head self-attention components to preserve the locality inductive biases of old tasks while inducing flexibility for new tasks in continual learning from tasks to tasks.  The proposed method is tested with a few recent MIM-based self-supervised methods (such as the MAE by He et al and SimMIM by Xie et al ) on ImageNet-1k which is split into 10 tasks each of which has 100 classes with promising results obtained.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

1) Continual self-supervised learning is an interesting yet under-explored problem. This paper presents a promising method for ViTs under the MIM-based setting. 
2) The proposed GLAD seems to be effective in experiments, although the improvement margin is not significant. 

Weaknesses:

1) The paper could be reorganized significantly. The proposed GLAD (Eqn.6) seems to be the only new component. However, it is not well motivated and explained. Among different parts in a Transformer block, why is the MHSA chosen and regularized in the proposed manner? 

2) The proposed method is tested on the ImageNet-1k split only. It's not clear how the split is done and how sensitive the method is to different ways of splits and different order of tasks in continual learning?  The last task in the 10-split is treated as non-iid task evaluation, which the reviewer is not sure when the split details are missing (e.g. it could be possible some of 100 classes in the last split are from the same super-category of classes in the first nine splits).  

3) Some of the presented results are not clear to the reviewer. E.g., how to understand Table 1? Is the performance on the first task T0 obtained by the model continually trained after the first nine tasks?

4) No downstream tasks are tested. For the baseline models (MAE and SimMIM), one of the motivations is their transferability to downstream tasks such as object detection and instance segmentation in MS-COCO. It's unclear how well the proposed continual learning variants will perform.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper could be improved significantly in terms of the focus of writing.  The evaluation results could be explained more clearly. The proposed GLAD module needs more justifications and/or analyses. The source code is provide but not verified by the reviewer.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper aims to address an important yet under-explored problem. The proposed GLAD intuitively makes senses. The experimental results are ok, but not sufficient. The reviewer would like to see the rebuttal on some of the weaknesses stated above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper performs an empirical analysis on the usefulness of supervised and unsupervised pre-training on a portion of tasks for effective continual learning downstream. The paper shows that full finetuning of a pre-trained model is effective for a downstream incremental task compared to only training a linear classifier over the pre-trained model. The paper then contributes an objective to increase the transferability of representations when pre-training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
-------------
+ The related work section of the paper is strong; it highlights relevant papers very well.
+ The objective proposed by the paper (GLAD) that maximizes the variance of attention weights is interesting and can potentially be a useful inspiration for work in other areas. 
+ One useful result that this paper provides is that fine-tuning the entire model works better than using a linear classifier for a downstream incremental task unseen during pre-training. This is useful, as typical self-supervised models are only linear probed during fine-tuning.
+ Another useful result this paper provides is that using a masked image modeling framework that results in learning more task-independent (or) generic (as shown by [1]) is useful in the continual learning setup.

[1] Zhenda Xie, Zigang Geng, Jingcheng Hu, Zheng Zhang, Han Hu, and Yue Cao. Revealing the dark secrets of masked image modeling. arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.13543, 2022a.

Weaknesses:
----------------
At the outset, the writing and presentation of the paper is poor. There are confusing passages in the text, and also some incorrect claims in the paper. The empirical evaluation is also insufficient as reported metrics are not the most relevant. The novelty does not seem upto typical ICLR standards. A detailed discussion of these issues follow.


**Methodology:**
* In Equation (2), why is D1:t−1 mentioned in the equation if data points of the previous tasks are not available? On similar lines, in Equation (3), why is X1:t−1 mentioned? If the paper means that the evaluation of the objective is done over D1:t−1 or X1:t−1, then the equations should be rewritten to be more clear.

* > Page 4: “While continual learning focuses on preserving local attention on past tasks to increment fine-grained problem-solving skills throughout training tasks sequentially, continual pre-training is about never-ending model generalization to achieve a better adaptation to the out-of-distribution task in the future.”

Q: There is confusion regarding use of the term “pre-training” throughout the paper. Continual pre-training without any context would mean that the (supposedly unlabelled) pre-training data arrives in an incremental fashion. Any unsupervised CL algorithm can handle this. What the paper means by “continual pre-training” here is that they would like to preserve the task-independent features through unsupervised continual learning, to ensure  that any downstream incremental task is benefitted maximally. It is important to make this point clear in the paper wherever the term “continual pre-training” has been used. This is important, considering the focus of this paper.

* > Page 4: “As Xie et al. (2022a) discussed both supervised (Sup) and contrastive self-supervised (SimSiam from Madaan et al. (2022)) frameworks train local attention at higher layers in neural networks, which is unsuitable for our motivation.”
	
Q: The paper should quote the specific point from Xie et al., as this argument forms the core motivation of the paper. The reader should not have to read Xie et al. to understand this paper.

* > Page 6: “We project the MSA features by multiplying a diagonal form of an adaptor diag(v) to maintain flexibility to address the current target task while constraining the multi-head attention to preserve locality inductive bias.”

Q: Why are GLAD adaptors necessary at all? Would it not work if the additional regularizer is applied without using any GLAD adaptors?

**Experimental results and metrics:**
* From the conducted analysis, It is unclear how the performance of continual pre-training scales with respect to dataset size (# classes), and also how it depends on # classes per task (i.e. the number of phases). It would be useful to: (i) Evaluate on one more dataset - ImageNet100 or CIFAR100; (ii) Evaluate on multiple task protocols. Conducting these two experiments may be necessary for thorough validation of the efficacy of continual pre-training 

* In Table 1, why measure performance on T0? Why not report average incremental accuracy that is reported in all CL works? Also, pre-training is done on 1K or 22K, and evaluation is also done on T0 which is Classes 1-100 of ImageNet? Has the model not already seen T0 (without the label), making the comparison unfair?

* Also, in Table 1, how is forward transfer measured? 

* In Figure 6, it is very difficult to infer what the values on the table are: are they task-specific accuracy values on T5/6/7/8 right after learning the specific tasks? In that case, these values are not useful in the CL setup. The average incremental accuracy over either all seen tasks so far (T0 → Tx) or all seen downstream tasks so far (T5 → Tx) should be reported.

* From the table in figure 6, I am unable to evaluate the usefulness of GLAD. The appropriate metrics should be reported.

**Incorrect/confusing claims:**
> Page 1: “However, the recently proposed UCL framework and its interpretations remain clear limitations from the point of view of model generalization.”

Q: It is unclear what “model generalization” means here. The average accuracy indicates generalization in the continual learning setup, and the interpretation of the UCL framework is clear from the UCL paper from a “generalization” viewpoint.

> Page 1: “ it cannot disclose the effect of knowledge transfer and adaptation of the model to the unseen target problems”.

Q: What is meant by ‘unseen target problems’?

> Page 1: “the transferability of continual (representation) learning models to the in- and out-of-distribution tasks”
Page 4: “However, we argue that such evaluation paradigms cannot appropriately measure the transferability of representation on unseen out-of-distribution problems.”

Q: CL tasks are always out-of-distribution to a model as they are unseen. If the paper means direct evaluation on unseen tasks without training on them, that is impossible as the respective classifier heads / linear heads for those classes would still need training.

> Figure 1(b): “ increases fine-tuning performance on the unseen task (T9).”. 

Q: It is confusing how ‘finetuning’ and ‘unseen’ appear together. A task that the model is ‘finetuned’ on may not be ‘unseen’. It may be better to refer to it as ‘downstream incremental task’ to indicate that it is an incremental task in the same stream, but is not part of pre-training.

> Page 2: “nullifying catastrophic forgetting”.

Q: The evaluation is done only on one task T9 that the model is finetuned on. This may not be an indicator of forgetting or not forgetting of previously seen tasks. It may be important to follow well-known metrics in continual learning to study forgetting.

> Page 2: “We explain these phenomena because the transferability hinges upon rich global features in pre-trained models, while the model mostly loses local features during CL, particularly severe when they train in a supervised/contrastive manner.”
Page 4: “model preserving the localized representation on pre-training tasks may not be beneficial for fine-tuning.”

Q: The term “local features” can be reworded as “task-specific features”, and “global features” as “task-generic/task-independent” features. These terms are repeated in various parts of the text, and must be replaced for clarity.

> Page 3: “Supervised Continual Learning (SCL) (Mallya & Lazebnik, 2018; Riemer et al., 2019; Aljundi et al., 2019; Chaudhry et al., 2019; 2020; Chrysakis & Moens, 2020; Titsias et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020; Douillard et al., 2022; Yoon et al., 2020; 2022) is about achieving forward positive transfer on unlimited sequential future tasks while maintaining proficiency on previous tasks.”

Q: I am not convinced with this statement. Supervised CL is not mainly about achieving forward positive transfer, but about maintaining performance on previous tasks, while also learning new tasks. 

> Page 5: “Our proposed UCL framework (SimMIM) obtains superior model generalization ability over other supervised and unsupervised counterparts”
	
Q: The paper incorrectly claims to have proposed SimMIM. SimMIM was proposed by Xie et al. (2022a) and the paper merely uses it in their experiments.

> Page 5: “our proposed framework outperforms supervised and contrastive benchmarks in model transferability during continual pre-training”.

Q: Section 4.2 describes the basic methodology used by any vision transformer. The paper has directly used this for continual learning. However the paper seems to claim this to be its own contribution.

> Page 7: “Masked Modeling focuses on capturing global attention rather than local attention, which provides a better generalization to adapt to unseen tasks but is inadequate for solving the problem.”
	
Q: This is confusing. The paper states that global attention is necessary to solve OOD tasks when finetuned, but here they state that it is “inadequate in solving the problem”.

> Page 6: “We construct a sequential dataset with nine earlier tasks and assign the last task as a validation set for non-iid task evaluation.”

This is misleading, as you cannot set the last task for zero-shot evaluation in the CL setup. I believe what is meant here is that the paper uses the first 9 tasks for pre-training and the 10th/last task for downstream finetuning.

Minor issues (not taken into account for rating):
------------------------------------------------------
* The term “increment” is used in many places with unclear context – other appropriate terms can be used eg. “increment the generalization of model representations” is not appropriate and the meaning is not clear.
* Page 2: “never-ending fine-tuning” → Fine-tuning in the literature usually means that the model is fine-tuned for one specific task. In the CL context I believe you mean ‘never-ending continual training’.
* Page 4: “I throw a question mark at this point:” → Use “we”.
* Page 13: There is a formatting error at “sup:subsec:analyses-vitswin”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The quality and clarity of the work is poor. The paper needs a complete end-to-end revision to be readable and useful. 

* There is marginal originality/novelty in the analysis conducted in the paper and the methodology (GLAD) proposed in the paper. It does not meet the ICLR bar.

* As for reproducibility, the hyperparameters used in the paper are reported, however there is no README or documentation in the code attached in the supplementary material. This makes the code hard to parse.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is riddled with incorrect claims and poor presentation that makes the paper difficult to read and evaluate. 

The analysis conducted and methodology proposed in the paper have marginal novelty and does not meet the ICLR bar.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a new task called “continual pre-training”, which aims to increment the generalization of model representations, encouraging positive transfer for future problems. Further, they propose a new method for continual pre-training: GLobal Attention Discretization (GLAD). Experiment results on ImageNet-1K are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

- Extensive experiment results are provided.
- The proposed method is technically sound. 

### Weakness 

- The continual pre-training benchmark protocol is not clearly defined in this paper. In supervised continual learning, there are many details when defining the benchmark protocol. For example, there is a memory constraint so we cannot save all historical samples. Some methods [A] allow a small memory buffer to save a small subset of the old samples. Can these detailed settings be applied to continual pre-training? The authors need to give discussions on these questions, provide a clear definition for the continual pre-training benchmark protocol, and explain the motivation. 

 

- The authors didn’t explain why the task “continual pre-training” is meaningful. We need continual learning because sometimes we have memory/privacy constraints and we cannot save all historical data. Why do we have similar constraints when pre-training the model? Usually, the pre-training stage is offline, and we don’t have any constraints on memory/privacy. If the above questions are not clearly explained, I don’t think the “continual pre-training” is meaningful.

 

- There are already some metrics for continual learning that show the transfer ability, e.g., the Forward Transfer in [B]. What is the difference between the existing metrics like “Forward Transfer” and the proposed task? Why do we need a new metric/benchmark to evaluate the transfer learning ability when designing a continual learning algorithm?

 

- There are some typos and grammar mistakes in the paper. For example, in the third line of the abstract, the correct sentence should be “However, most recent works on continual learning focus on …”

 

[A] Rebuffi, Sylvestre-Alvise, et al. "icarl: Incremental classifier and representation learning." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2017.

[B] Lopez-Paz, David, and Marc'Aurelio Ranzato. "Gradient episodic memory for continual learning." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity & Quality

Some important motivations (e.g., why continual pre-training is meaningful) are not explained. Many details on the continual pre-training benchmark protocol are not discussed. 

### Novelty 

The authors propose a novel task and an algorithm for the proposed task. However, the proposed task is similar to some existing continual learning metrics, e.g., Forward Transfer in [B].

### Reproducibility

The authors provide the code in the supplementary.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this paper is interesting. However, many important details and motivations are missing. I will consider upgrading my rating after seeing the rebuttal.

content.title: Continual Pre-trainer is an Incremental Model Generalizer
content.TL;DR: In this paper, we tackle a novel problem of Continual Pre-training, which aims to increment the generalization of model representations, encouraging positive transfer for future problems.
content.abstract:
With the necessity of lifelong-learnable machines over continuously changing real-world problems in practice, there has been rapid progress in continual learning these days. However, most recent works on continual learning focuses on alleviating catastrophic forgetting of a model trained over a sequence of vision tasks, considering only the performance on the tasks themselves rather than the representation transferability.
In this paper, we tackle a novel problem of Continual Pre-training, which aims to increment the generalization of model representations, encouraging positive transfer for future problems. An initial empirical study shows a rather surprising finding that the transfer quality of the pre-trained model representation with both supervised and unsupervised task sequences does not show noticeable performance degradation even with full-finetuning.
Furthermore, we propose a simple yet efficient Continual Pre-training method with GLobal Attention Discretization (GLAD) which introduces a new constraint to increment the global transferability of the backbone while projecting model weights to adapt to target problems via additional weight vectors. Our continual pretraining method breaks the barriers between pre-training and fine-tuning steps and leads to an integrated design that combines continual representation learning with continual learning of the task-specific learners.
